In 1682, the Ottoman Empire controlled more European territory than at any point before or since — Hungary, the Balkans, and vassal states stretching to the Black Sea.

One year later, it overreached. a thread 🧵🗺️

1/ This map is the high-water mark. Ottoman Hungary, plus Transylvania, Wallachia and Moldavia as vassals, and the Crimean Khanate as an ally — the empire's northern border sat closer to Vienna than at any time in its history.

2/ Look at the rest of the board: Sweden still ruled a Baltic empire, Russia was only a "Tsardom" (the title "Russian Empire" was four decades away), and Poland-Lithuania was still one of the largest states in Europe by area.

3/ The Holy Roman Empire, shown here as a patchwork of "other states" around a shrunken core, held well over 300 semi-independent territories — a fragmented Germany that wouldn't unify for another 189 years.

4/ In 1683, Grand Vizier Kara Mustafa Pasha pushed the Ottoman border one step further and besieged Vienna itself. On September 12, a relief army led by Poland's King Jan III Sobieski broke the siege — the closest the Ottomans ever came to taking the city.

5/ That defeat triggered the Great Turkish War (1683-1699). By the Treaty of Karlowitz in 1699, the Ottomans had ceded most of Hungary and Transylvania to the Habsburgs — their first major territorial loss in Europe after nearly 300 years of expansion.

6/ This map is the moment right before the tide turned — the Ottoman Empire never again held this much of Europe.
